title: Choosing a training split: full body, upper/lower, push-pull-legs
chunks: A training split is how you divide your muscles across the week. There is no single best split — the best one is the one that fits your schedule, lets you train each muscle about twice a week, and that you can stick to consistently. Frequency and total volume matter more than the specific split.

Full-body training works each major muscle group every session and suits people training 2–3 days a week. It delivers high frequency per muscle and is very time-efficient, though sessions can feel long if you include many exercises.

An upper/lower split alternates upper-body and lower-body days, fitting well into 4 days a week. It lets you train each muscle twice weekly with enough volume per session and is a reliable default for intermediates.

Push/pull/legs (PPL) groups pushing muscles (chest, shoulders, triceps), pulling muscles (back, biceps), and legs. Run over 6 days it trains each muscle twice a week with high volume; run over 3 days it trains each once. PPL suits people who enjoy higher gym frequency.

A 'bro split' trains one muscle group per day (chest day, back day, etc.) with only once-weekly frequency per muscle. It can build muscle but is generally less efficient than training each muscle about twice a week, so it is not the best starting choice for most people.

Match the split to your real availability. If you can reliably train 3 days, a full-body or upper/lower/full setup beats an ambitious 6-day plan you will miss. Consistency over months is what builds muscle, not the theoretical perfection of the program.

Whatever the split, aim to hit each muscle group roughly twice per week, keep weekly sets per muscle in a productive range, and apply progressive overload. The split is just the container; what fills it — volume, intensity, and progression — drives results.
